having denied her, according to Paul's voice, they plunder the minds of the simple, leading them astray with deceitful words, and persuading them to fall into the snare of death and the trap of Hades, as it is written; for they should not add to what they know, but rather follow their own vain thoughts, not knowing what they say or about what they are speaking; but you, stay in what you have learned, as Paul says, avoiding empty disputes, and holding the faith in simple thoughts, and the tradition of the Church as a precious treasure, having the teachings that please God; so that you may not only be shining in faith, but also be conspicuous in the virtues that have been accomplished in piety; for the path to virtue is difficult, but the command to love one's neighbor as oneself is the key to all our goodness, and it is not hard to demonstrate; for Paul, the wisest, exhorts us to owe nothing to anyone, except to love one another

For the one loving the other has fulfilled the law. For: Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in the word: Love your neighbor as yourself. The love of the neighbor does no evil. The love is the fulfillment of the law. You hear how the entire word is enclosed in the definition of love. For all the things of the deeds that seem to have transcended the divine law, these have certainly fallen outside the circles of love. To those who ought to be admired, it is seen that love is present, to see through deeds inside love. For the one doing injustice does not love the neighbor; the one hating injustice loves, of course, in every way, fulfilling the entire law. For the love that hastens to honor the things in the law brings about fulfillment; sloth, however, has the origin of the things accused by the law. For who would, tell me, approach the wife of someone and rush into foreign marriages, wishing to grieve someone out of love? Who, I think, would not avoid murdering, restrained by all strength, shame, and honor towards the one persuaded, as if by some bridle towards gentleness? To what of the existing things would not the creation of the aliens be seen as detestable and most hateful, thinking it bitter and placing it among the most shameful evils, to harm a brother? Therefore, the law that turns us towards all virtue has its fulfillment in love.

But I think it is fitting to examine more carefully the parts of the virtue recently named by us, what it is that results from it. Therefore, I will use the voice of Paul; love is patient, love is kind; love does not envy; love does not boast, is not puffed up, does not behave indecently, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not keep a record of wrongs, does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails. You see how great a multitude of good things the power of love brings to us. Love is patient, that is, it does not become weak towards the neighbor's lack of courage; for the one who is patient in every way also endures some of the unreasonable things done to him by others, and he struggles against some of the things that cause pain.

But better than those who are grieved and appear after this, they reap the benefit of all good things. For what is the most beautiful thing about love has passed by in a small moment. For what does the advocate of virtue say again about it, what does he urge another of the worthy to accomplish, let us examine again. Love, he says, does not seek its own, does not become angry. The precise and more legal word in these things would show that one who does not seek his own, who has made nothing his own, does not seek his own until what is useful to the many has been revealed to him. For example, I say, give to go out and through examples the word. For the leaders of the Jewish factions once commanded the holy apostles not to speak to anyone in the name of Christ, but they, having disregarded those who were speaking nonsense, and although dangers were hanging over them, again taught the crowds, urging that it was fitting for those who had been deceived to be corrected, having rightly judged, but completely disregarding the irrational plot from there. For they did not seek their own, but the things of others, not going beyond the boundary of the love of God. But if the preceding passage demands some such theory from us, but if we are accustomed to think more simply, let us turn back to it again, applying the words of the Savior.

Therefore, leading us to the highest point, gentleness, and brotherly love, and the desire for nothing, and the thorny passion of our soul, 'Give to everyone who asks you'; and 'do not demand back from the one who takes your things'. You hear how it commands to forgive the stranger; no one will take away from us what is just, wanting to resist; but rather to seem better and to be stirred up by the removal of goods, that is, by those who are being taken away by chance, and to be inflamed with unseemly anger. But what will the robber say to me again? The one who is established in the ways of a beast, and the one who has not done wrong, as if one of the enemies, running alongside, and having spread the sail of robbery in the rivers, and even if someone is caught, immediately jumping up, and being inflamed with unnatural boldness. Where have you placed, tell me, the law of the Savior, although you say you are a Christian? You are walking around the ordinance of love; but as if you have been transformed into a wild beast, and having fallen into unnatural savagery, you no longer feel. But the one who has become according to the divine image, having not arranged in the logic of no one, you do not know; but you dare to strike unjustly with iron.

but sowing a dead thing on the earth when seeing a person of the same kind as you, you do not immediately hand it over to them, nor do you reckon with those who are so savage in their boldness, as they have become accustomed to plowing the earth, to cut up the furrows with plows, then to hide in them what is sown, and again to reap what has been brought to maturity by God, and you marvel at the earth here, as the mother of good fruits, as serving you best for the provision of necessities, and you praise, as is fitting, the use of iron, how then do you not blush at the injustices through which you have life, for you have made the one a murderer, and the other you have defiled with the blood of the innocent, how then do you still invite the earth to become a mother of fruits for you, if you have been unjust and unmerciful, how will you touch the bright iron, which, having perverted from its proper use, you have made a murderer
pass_b_english: Those who have denied the truth plunder the minds of the simple, leading them astray with deceitful words and persuading them to fall into the snare of death and the trap of Hades, as it is written.
They should not add to what they know, but rather follow their own vain thoughts, not knowing what they say or about what they are speaking, because they are ignorant of the truth.

In contrast, we should stay in what we have learned, avoiding empty disputes and holding the faith in simple thoughts, as Paul says, and holding the tradition of the Church as a precious treasure, having the teachings that please God.

The path to virtue is difficult, but the command to love one's neighbor as oneself is the key to all our goodness, and it is not hard to demonstrate, for Paul, the wisest, exhorts us to owe nothing to anyone, except to love one another.

The one who loves the other has fulfilled the law, for love is the foundation of all commandments, including 'Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not covet,' as it is summed up in the word: 'Love your neighbor as yourself'.

The love of the neighbor does no evil, and it is the fulfillment of the law, for the entire word of God is enclosed in the definition of love, and all deeds that seem to have transcended the divine law have fallen outside the circles of love.

Love is present in those who ought to be admired, and it is seen through their deeds, for the one who does injustice does not love the neighbor, but the one who hates injustice loves, fulfilling the entire law, because the love that hastens to honor the things in the law brings about fulfillment, while sloth has the origin of the things accused by the law.

The virtue of love is a multifaceted one, and it is essential to examine its various aspects carefully, for as Paul so eloquently puts it, 'Love is patient, love is kind; love does not envy; love does not boast, is not puffed up, does not behave indecently, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not keep a record of wrongs, does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth'.
Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things, and it never fails, for the power of love brings a multitude of good things to our lives.

When we consider the nature of love, we see that it is patient, even in the face of our neighbor's lack of courage, and the patient person endures unreasonable things done to them by others and struggles against the things that cause pain.

For example, when the leaders of the Jewish factions commanded the holy apostles not to speak to anyone in the name of Christ, they, having disregarded this command and despite dangers hanging over them, continued to teach the crowds, urging them to be corrected and to turn away from their deception, because they did not seek their own interests, but rather the things of others, and they did not go beyond the boundary of the love of God.

As we strive for the highest point of gentleness and brotherly love, we must also consider the desire for nothing and the thorny passion of our soul, for Jesus taught us, saying, 'Give to everyone who asks you, and do not demand back from the one who takes your things'.

You marvel at the earth's ability to produce good fruits, and you praise the use of iron, which is essential for your survival, but you do not blush at the injustices you have committed, which have given you life, for you have made one thing a murderer and defiled another with the blood of the innocent.

How can you still expect the earth to produce fruits for you if you have been unjust and unmerciful, and how can you touch the bright iron, which you have perverted from its proper use and made a murderer?

For the one who has become according to the divine image, having not arranged in the logic of no one, you do not know, but you dare to strike unjustly with iron, and you do not feel, because you have been transformed into a wild beast, and having fallen into unnatural savagery, you walk in the ways of a beast.
